html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. AI: artificial intelligence; PII: personally identifiable information; LLM: large language model; ZDR: zero data retention; BAA: business associate agreement; MCP: Model Context Protocol

  • How to turn a vague business ask into a testable problem statement
  • How to decide whether Claude is the right tool and which solution shape fits
  • The five business value pillars and how to attach measurable targets to them
  • How to frame constraints and risks before design starts

2From Ask to Problem Statement

Running case

Lumen Advisory and the Bank That Wants "AI for Customer Service"

  • A retail bank's executive says: "We want AI in customer service."
  • Lumen's architect asks what hurts: average handle time, inconsistent answers, after-hours coverage, cost per contact
  • The ask becomes: draft replies for agents from the policy library, with citations, cut handle time 25 percent, no regulated advice without review

A business ask is a wish; a problem statement names who, what, how well, under which constraints.

Element Question Bank example
Users and workflow Who will use it, in which process step? Contact-center agents drafting replies
Pain and baseline What is wrong today, in numbers? 9-minute handle time, 14 percent rework
Success criteria What result counts as success, measurably? 25 percent faster, 95 percent policy-correct
Constraints Latency, cost, data, regulation, platform, skills Customer PII, region rules, budget per contact
Risks What happens when it is wrong? Wrong fee advice reaches a customer
Ownership Who accepts, runs and funds it? Head of service operations
  • Success criteria first. Specific, measurable, achievable and relevant criteria are the basis of later evals (Module 11).
  • Translate language to metrics: "faster" becomes handle time; "accurate" becomes policy-correct rate on a test set.
  • Fit check: LLMs suit language-heavy, variable, judgment-assisted work; they are a poor first choice for exact, rule-bound calculation, hard real-time control, or tasks where a simple rule or classic model is cheaper and fully reliable.
Exam tip

The first architect move on a vague request is discovery that produces measurable success criteria and constraints, not choosing a model or a framework.

3Choosing the Solution Shape

Shape Use when Cost and risk
Single optimized call Task fits one prompt with good context and examples Lowest
Workflow (chain, route, parallel) Steps are known; each can be checked Low; predictable
Augmented LLM (retrieval, tools, memory) Needs your data or actions Medium; integration and security work
Agent / multi-agent Path cannot be predicted in advance Highest; compounding errors, 4x to 15x tokens
  • Simplest solution that works: add complexity only when it demonstrably improves the measured outcome.
  • Build, buy or configure: use built-in product features where they meet the need; build custom only for differentiating or constrained cases.
  • Plan where a human reviews: draft-and-review is usually the first production pattern for risky outputs.

4Business Value Pillars

The guide names five pillars. Tie every design choice to at least one and give it a number.

Pillar Meaning Example target Typical design lever
Efficiency Same output with less time or effort Handle time down 25% Draft generation, retrieval of policy
Transformation New capability or redesigned process Instant multilingual support New workflow, agentic process
Productivity More output per person Analyst reviews 3x more files Summarization, extraction
Cost Lower total cost to serve Cost per contact down 30% Smaller model, caching, batch
Performance SLAs Meet speed, availability, quality commitments p95 latency under 3 seconds, 99.9% uptime Streaming, routing, capacity planning

  • Pillars conflict: a larger model may raise quality but lift cost and latency. State the priority order with the client.
  • Quantify benefit and cost early (tokens per request times volume, review effort, integration work) to test the business case.
Exam tip

A design justified by a named pillar with a measurable target is stronger than one justified by "better AI". When pillars conflict, the answer states the trade-off and the client's priority.

5Constraints That Shape the Design

Constraint Effect on design
Data sensitivity and regulation Platform and region choice, ZDR or BAA, PII masking (Module 14)
Latency Streaming, smaller model, caching, routing (Module 10)
Volume and cost Batch, caching, model tiering (Modules 4, 6, 12)
Existing systems Integration path: API, MCP, queue (Modules 7, 8)
Team skills and operations Managed services, simpler patterns, runbooks (Module 16)
Accuracy and risk tolerance Evals, human review, guardrails (Modules 11, 13)
Exam tip

Pillars conflict (quality against cost and latency): the strong answer names the trade-off and the client's priority.

6Exam Q&A

S1A client says "we want AI in customer service." What should the architect do first?

  • ABuild a multi-agent system so that every future requirement can be absorbed without redesigning anything later
  • BRun structured discovery to define users, baseline metrics, success criteria and constraints
  • CCompare vendor pricing and select the cheapest model before talking to anyone
  • DChoose the most capable model and start prototyping an autonomous support agent for the contact center
Show the answer

Answer: B. Measurable criteria and constraints must exist before architecture choices.

S2A task has fixed steps, each easy to check, and low tolerance for unpredictability. Which shape fits?

  • AA workflow such as prompt chaining with checks between steps
  • BA multi-agent system with a coordinator and several specialist agents
  • CA single prompt with no intermediate validation to keep latency minimal
  • DA fully autonomous agent that decides its own path at every step
Show the answer

Answer: A. Known steps favor a predictable workflow over an agent.

S3An executive wants an "AI transformation" but cannot name a metric. Which response is best?

  • ATie the initiative to a pillar with a measurable target and a baseline, and agree the priority among pillars
  • BDefer all measurement until the system is live and users have formed opinions
  • CAgree a broad vision statement and let the engineering team choose measures later
  • DStart with the newest model and demonstrate impressive examples to the sponsor to build enthusiasm for the project
Show the answer

Answer: A. Business value must be measurable to guide design and to judge success.

S4Which task is the weakest fit for an LLM as the core component?

  • ASummarizing long case notes for a human reviewer
  • BExact interest calculation that must be reproducible to the cent
  • CDrafting replies to varied customer emails from a policy library
  • DClassifying incoming requests that arrive in free text
Show the answer

Answer: B. Exact, rule-bound calculation belongs in deterministic code; the LLM can orchestrate or explain.

S5A larger model raises quality but breaks the p95 latency target. How should the architect proceed?

  • APresent the quality-latency trade-off, confirm the client's priority, and test routing or a smaller model with caching
  • BSwitch to the smallest model without testing because latency is a hard constraint
  • CKeep the larger model and ask the client to relax the latency target without evidence
  • DRemove the latency target from the requirements to simplify the design
Show the answer

Answer: A. Pillars conflict; make the trade-off explicit and test options against it.

S6Which TWO belong in a problem statement before design begins? Select TWO.

  • AThe brand of the vector database that will be used
  • BConstraints such as data sensitivity, latency and regulation
  • CThe number of agents the final design will contain
  • DThe exact wording of the system prompt
  • EA baseline and a measurable target for the business outcome
Show the answer

Answer: B, E. Targets and constraints frame the design; implementation details come later.

S7When is a multi-agent design most justified?

  • AAny task where several steps exist, because more agents always raise quality
  • BSmall tasks with strong dependencies between steps and shared context
  • CHigh-value work that parallelizes well and exceeds a single context window
  • DCost-sensitive high-volume classification with a fixed label set
Show the answer

Answer: C. Multi-agent systems cost many more tokens and suit parallelizable, high-value work.

S8The bank wants to cut cost per contact. Which design lever most directly serves the cost pillar?

  • ACaching the stable policy prefix and routing simple requests to a smaller model
  • BAdding more agents so that each contact is handled by a specialist
  • CExpanding the context with every available policy document on each call, so that nothing is ever missing
  • DIncreasing effort for every request to reduce rework
Show the answer

Answer: A. Caching and tiering reduce the cost per request without discarding needed context.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
First move Discovery to measurable success criteria and constraints
Problem statement Users · pain and baseline · target · constraints · risks · owner
Fit Language-heavy, variable work; not exact calculation or hard real-time
Shapes Single call · workflow · augmented LLM · agent or multi-agent
Rule Simplest that works; climb only on evidence
Pillars Efficiency · transformation · productivity · cost · performance SLAs
Conflict State the trade-off and the client's priority
Human review Plan it where errors are costly
